title: Handling parent complaints with a clear procedure
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals on setting up a simple, fair complaints procedure so parent concerns are resolved early instead of escalating.
body:
Every school gets complaints. The difference between a school that handles them well and one that does not is rarely the complaint itself. It is whether the parent can see a clear route, a fair hearing, and a response.

A simple written procedure turns complaints from a source of conflict into useful information.

Treat complaints as information

A parent complaint often points to something real: a communication gap, an unfair decision, a facility problem. Schools that treat complaints as attacks respond defensively. Schools that treat them as feedback fix problems earlier and keep parents on side.

A simple route to follow

  • Level one: the class teacher or head of department, for most day-to-day concerns.
  • Level two: the deputy principal, if the issue is not resolved or is more serious.
  • Level three: the principal.
  • Final level: the BOM, and where needed, the Sub-County Director of Education.

Respond to the emotion before the issue: A parent who feels heard will often accept an answer they did not want. A parent who feels dismissed will escalate even when the facts favour the school.

Acknowledge quickly, respond properly

Acknowledge every complaint within a day or two, even if the full answer takes longer, and say when the parent can expect a response. Silence is what turns small concerns into formal escalations.

Be fair and keep records

Listen to all sides before deciding. Keep complaint details confidential. Write down what was raised, what was done, and the outcome. A written record protects the parent, the teacher, and the school.

Review complaint patterns every term.

Once a term, look at what complaints you received. Repeated concerns about fees, food, or communication point to a system problem worth fixing.
